summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules govern entry into Niue, while criminal liability is determined by Niue's own statute law.

Sexual conduct between men was criminalised under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code, which covered buggery, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males and carried penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment. Those provisions were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue achieved self-governance in 1974, and left untouched by New Zealand's own decriminalisation in 1986, which amended New Zealand law only. The Niue Assembly subsequently passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May, in force in June, repealing them (Human Dignity Trust).

No source in the current inventory records criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct in Niue today, and none documents enforcement against queer people. The jurisdiction carries no statutory protection either: there is no non-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex relationships or marriages, and no recorded bias-motivated-violence framework.

The age of consent was equalised in May 2011 according to ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey. The Niue Act 1966, Part 21 (Marriage of Minors), still sets the age of majority at 21 for men and 19 for women, a sex-asymmetric threshold that remained on the statute books as of that survey and bears on capacity to marry and related legal thresholds.

UN Free & Equal's August 2015 information sheet for the Pacific lists Niue's fakafifine among the diverse pre-colonial gender identities of the area, described as "important parts of the cultural treasure of the region". The identity is documented as deeply embedded in family life, coexisting with a church-led conservative social environment.
tangentialFactors:
Niue is one of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand. Its decriminalisation history runs on a separate track from New Zealand's: the 1986 reform of New Zealand law had no effect here, and the local repeal came later, which means comparative references to New Zealand's legal position do not describe what applies on the ground.

The documentary base is thin. No audited source records any enforcement action against queer people in either direction, so the absence of documented prosecutions should be read as an absence of evidence rather than as evidence of practice. The source inventory also does not state the year in which the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act was passed, only the month of passage and of commencement.

The sex-asymmetric age of majority in the Niue Act 1966 is a legacy anomaly visible on the face of the principal statute, and it persisted into the 2010s alongside otherwise equalised consent ages.
localsOnly:
Residents live with the same protection gap as visitors: no non-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no statutory recognition exists for same-sex relationships, so grievances of that kind have no domestic legal route.

The Niue Act 1966, Part 21 (Marriage of Minors), fixes the age of majority at 21 for men and 19 for women. The asymmetry applies to residents' own capacity questions, not to visitors alone, and it remained on the books as of the May 2011 ILGA survey.

Fakafifine is documented by UN Free & Equal (August 2015) as a pre-colonial gender identity of Niue and an important part of the region's cultural treasure, embedded in family structures and coexisting with church-led conservatism. Local gender nonconformity therefore has an established cultural referent, even without legal recognition or protection.

Criminal law as amended by the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act governs the conduct of residents; the repeal of the former ss.43-44 offences applies to everyone within the jurisdiction.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced material on legal gender recognition or the rules for changing sex markers on passports and birth records; entry documents are governed by New Zealand nationality and passport rules, but marker-change procedure is not documented here.

No sourced information covers restroom or facility access, screening practices that could disclose a visitor's trans status, access to gender-affirming or general healthcare, or any public-health provision addressing gender identity or sexual behaviour. Whether such provisions exist is unresolved on this record.

Hate-crime or bias-motivated violence protections, and any enforcement statistics for them, are not sourced. The claim that no enforcement against queer people is documented rests on the absence of such material in the inventory, not on an affirmative finding of non-enforcement.

The year of passage and commencement of the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act is not stated in the sources; only the month of each is given. The precise current wording of the Niue Act 1966 marriage provisions, and whether later amendments altered the 21/19 ages of majority, is likewise unresolved.
